paper_title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose CoPE, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, CoPE trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, $τ^2$-bench, and AppWorld), CoPE (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to $1.9\times$ and $2.0\times$ higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead. The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks such as web navigation (Zheng et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), agentic coding (Yang et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2023; Sapkota et al., 2025), and scientific discovery (Zheng et al., 2025; Buehler, 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025). However, training these agents remains computationally expensive. Because each rollout involves numerous interaction steps and tool calls, extracting the maximum learning signal from limited number of interactions is crucial (Liu & van der Schaar, 2025). Yet, standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often learns only from single scalar reward at the end of trajectory, leaving stepwise supervision in the process, such as intermediate actions and environment observations, largely unused. To exploit more intermediate supervision from the process, prior work constructs two kinds of additional targets. Value targets are estimates of how likely each intermediate step is to lead to success, obtained from process reward models (Choudhury, 2025; Xi et al., 2026) or step-level credit assignment (Feng et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026), and serve as dense rewards or advantages. Observation targets are the environments next observation or state. Some methods fit separate LLM world model to them and use it to plan or to synthesize additional experience (Chen et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026); others fit them as an auxiliary objective of the policy backbone, before or alongside policy optimization (Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). *Equal contribution.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: Motivation of COPE for sample-efficient RL. (a) terminal observation contains many task-irrelevant tokens, whereas the corresponding action is short and decision-relevant. (b) Three kinds of targets at the same history ht. Value targets are shared across steps: every step of trajectory is labeled with the same final outcome . The observation target ˆot+1 is noisy and reaches only one step ahead. COPEs action targets condition on = 1 and are specific to each step: ht is labeled with the actions that actually followed it, at:t+K (K = 3 here), and the next step with at+1:t+K+1. (c) On AppWorld, COPE reaches training task score of 0.5 with 1.6 fewer RL steps than GRPO. Key challenges. Both existing prediction targets are difficult to construct effectively in complex agentic environments. (1) Value targets are derived from only the shared outcome. trajectory records only its final outcome, not the success probability of each step, so every step is labeled with this same outcome, whose randomness comes mostly from later actions and observations rather than from the step itself. Distinguishing between steps requires step-level annotations, additional rollouts from intermediate states, or exact recurrence of states across rollouts. (2) Observation targets are noisy and reach only one step ahead. In web navigation or agentic coding, most tokens of the next observation (e.g., HTML DOM trees or verbose terminal logs) are irrelevant to the decision (Fig. 1a), so the prediction loss is dominated by reproducing them. The target also covers only single-step transition; reaching later steps requires chaining predictions, where errors compound. Our solution. We propose COPE, which constructs third kind of target: multi-step action targets. Alongside GRPO, COPE employs multi-step action forecasting on successful on-policy trajectories, predicting actions at:t+K directly from the current history while skipping the intervening observations. We show that the population optimum of this objective is Pr(at:t+K ht, success), hindsight distribution (Harutyunyan et al., 2019; Russo, 2026) that conditions on both the history and the episodes eventual success. Success thus enters as condition that selects trajectories, not as label assigned to each step. Therefore, COPE overcomes previous limitations in three key ways. (1) Action targets are specific to each step. successful trajectory labels each step with its own continuation, the actions that actually followed it. (2) Action targets are decision-relevant. Actions are concise (Fig. 1a), so the loss is not spent on irrelevant observation content. (3) Multi-step action targets span the horizon and form an implicit temporal ensemble. Each action is supervised both where it is taken and when it is forecast from the preceding histories, and the shared backbone absorbs this ensemble into the policy through training alone. This agrees with the delay view of action chunking in robot learning, where predicting chunks trains each action from the current and several earlier observations; the resulting ensemble of delayed predictors, which ACT averages explicitly at test time (Zhao et al., 2023), accounts for much of chunkings benefit (Lazzati et al., 2026). COPE differs by still acting one step at time at inference, with no overhead. Main findings. We evaluate COPE on five benchmarks spanning three simulated environments (ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022), and WebShop (Yao et al., 2022)) and two realistic applications (τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024)). Our experiments yield three main findings. (1) Broad improvements: COPE outperforms GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and observation-prediction baselines (ECHO (Shrivastava et al., 2026) and RWML (Yu et al., 2026)) on aggregate metrics in the three simulated environments, and improves overall metrics on both realistic applications (despite negative result on the Airline domain of τ 2bench). (2) Sample efficiency: on ScienceWorld, COPE is up to 1.9 and 2.0 more sample-efficient than ECHO and GRPO, respectively. (3) Low overhead: on ScienceWorld, the action forecasting pass adds just 11% time per training step on average, while shorter rollouts reduce the measured end-to-end step time by 9%; COPE requires neither separate model nor pretraining stage.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Sample-efficient agentic RL. Methods for sample-efficient agentic RL follow two main directions. The first makes better use of outcome rewards, either by refining credit assignment within trajectories (Feng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Kong et al., 2026) or by converting completed interactions into extra policy supervision via hindsight rewriting or on-policy distillation (Hu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). These methods change how sparse outcomes are assigned or reused, without necessarily introducing predictive objective. The second learns from the environment feedback available at every step, typically by adding auxiliary prediction of future states or observations to policy training (Zhang et al., 2026; Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Such objectives provide dense token-level supervision but generally focus on single environment transition. COPE combines elements of both directions: success filtering reuses outcome rewards, while multi-horizon prediction learns from how trajectories unfold in action space rather than reconstructing observations. Multi-horizon prediction. COPE is closely related to several forms of multi-horizon and outcomeconditioned prediction. Multi-token prediction trains language models to predict several future tokens (Gloeckle et al., 2024), while robotic policies such as ACT and Diffusion Policy predict sequences of future actions (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023). Multi-token prediction is closest architecturally because multiple offsets are learned by one backbone, whereas action chunking is closest in the structure of its targets. Outcome-conditioned sequence modeling conditions policies on desired returns, while self-imitation emphasizes high-return trajectories (Chen et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2018); both connect policy learning to trajectory-level outcomes. Accordingly, the = 0 term in COPE is success-filtered imitation, while the 1 terms extend this supervision to multiple future action offsets. COPE uses these predictions as an auxiliary objective during on-policy GRPO: targets are regenerated from successful rollouts, and the predicted future actions are not executed as chunk but affect acting through the shared backbone.

sections.title: 5.1 SHARING PARAMETERS FOR ACTING AND FORECASTING
sections.content: We instantiate both the acting policy πθ and the action forecaster pθ on single LLM backbone θ: πθ(at ht) is the models next-action distribution given history ht, whereas pθ(at:t+K ht) is the distribution over action chunks generated when forecasting instruction is appended to ht. Because of this forecasting instruction, pθ and πθ are distinct distributions: even at the first forecast position (K = 0), pθ(at ht) does not generally equal πθ(at ht). Sharing the backbone offers two key benefits: (1) No additional model. Forecasting reuses the policys parameters, requiring no separate model to train, store, or serve. (2) Shared representation. Multi-step structure captured by the forecasting objective is written directly into the representation from which the policy acts, allowing acting and forecasting to co-evolve (Sec. 5.3).

sections.content: Acting helps forecasting via trajectory collection. For fixed rollout policy π and sufficiently expressive model, LAF(θ) is minimized on every history reached by successful rollouts by the hindsight action chunk itself (Eq. 4), which by Bayes rule is pθ (at:t+K ht) = q(at:t+K ht) Prπ(at:t+K ht) Prπ(Y = 1 ht, at:t+K). (6) The first factor represents the action chunks proposed by the policy π, and the second is their success probability (value), which success filtering enforces via rejection sampling. This reweighting keeps the target ahead of the generating policy: acting at every history according to the single-step marginal q(at ht) succeeds at least as often as acting with π (Russo, 2026). Since both factors depend on the current policy π, forecasting relies on acting to supply successful rollouts and receives more of them as the policy improves. Forecasting helps acting via implicit temporal ensembling. Sec. 4 views the forecasting loss along each row of Fig. 2(ii): each history ht must anticipate its future chunk at:t+K. Viewed along each column, every action at of successful rollout also lies within the chunks of the preceding histories, receiving supervision from each of ht, ht1, . . . , htK through the forecast pθ(at htk, atk:t1), rather than only from ht at the moment it is executed as in GRPO. These forecasts do not conflict with acting: since all are conditionals of the same hindsight distribution Pr+, the optimal forecast of at issued at htk equals the GRPO target q(at ht) marginalized over the intermediate observations between and t. Because the forecaster shares θ with the acting policy (Sec. 5.1), these earlier forecasts are implicitly ensembled into πθ through the shared representation (see Sec. 8). Joint optimization and inference. We optimize the shared parameters with L(θ) = ˆLGRPO(θ) + λ ˆLAF(θ), where ˆLAF is given by Eq. 5 and λ is weighting hyperparameter (Alg. 1). The forecasting objective is used only during training: at inference, the agent acts with πθ alone, generating one action per step without the forecasting instruction, so COPE adds no inference cost over GRPO-trained policy.

sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS
sections.content: Tasks. We evaluate on five long-horizon agent benchmarks with sparse rewards that differ in observation complexity, action space, and horizon. Three are simulated environments: (1) ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) for household tasks, (2) ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) for elementary science experiments, and (3) WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) for online shopping over long web-page observations. Two are realistic applications: (1) τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) for policy-constrained customer service with user simulator, and (2) AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) for composing API calls across consumer apps with code as actions. We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2024) for the three simulated environments and τ 2-bench, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for the more difficult AppWorld tasks. Details are available in Appendix A. Unless otherwise stated, all analysis experiments are carried out on ScienceWorld. Baselines. On the simulated environments  (Table 3)  , we compare against three groups. (1) Prompting: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite (Comanici et al., 2025), GPT-5-mini and GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2025; 2026), and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), which adds verbal self-reflection on failed trials. (2) RL w/o auxiliary loss: RFT (Yuan et al., 2023), rejection sampling fine-tuning; GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), critic-free RL with group-normalized advantages; and EMPG (Wang et al., 2025), which rescales GRPOs step-level gradients by policy entropy. (3) RL w/ auxiliary loss: RWML (Yu et al., 2026), which first trains next-state prediction on environment transitions and then runs GRPO; and ECHO (Shrivastava et al., 2026), which adds next-observation prediction loss to GRPO. Both supervise only single-step transitions, testing whether forecasting actions over multiple steps is more effective than predicting the next observation. On τ 2-bench and AppWorld (Tables 1 and 2), we include published baseline numbers reported by G2PO (Wang et al., 2026a) and InfoPO (Kong et al., 2026), together with GRPO and COPE runs from our implementation. Because the published AppWorld results use different task subset and protocol (Appendix B.1), our direct comparison is between GRPO (ours) and COPE under our shared setup.

sections.content: COPE achieves aggregate gains across five agentic benchmarks. Across both simulated and realistic agentic tasks, COPE improves the benchmark-level aggregate metrics over GRPO. On

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: ALFWorld  (Table 3)  , COPE improves performance by 5.0 points over GRPO. The gains are larger on WebShop and ScienceWorld, where success rates increase by 12.5 points to 77.0% and by 8.0 points to 72.5%, respectively; on ScienceWorld, COPE also achieves the best performance among the RL-based methods. The same trend largely extends to more realistic benchmarks. On τ 2-bench  (Table 1)  , COPE improves overall success from 27.5% to 28.7%, driven by an approximately 12-point gain on Retail, despite drop on Airline. We analyze the drop in Sec. 8. Finally, on AppWorld  (Table 2)  , COPE substantially improves over GRPO on both splits, increasing success from 41.67% to 55.36% on the normal split and from 18.71% to 22.54% on the challenge split. COPE outperforms observation-based auxiliary losses on aggregate simulated-task metrics. On the three simulated environments where ECHO and RWML are evaluated, COPE achieves the best aggregate results. It exceeds the stronger baseline by 1.0 point on ALFWorld, by 4.4 average-score points and 5.5 success-rate points on WebShop, and by 5.0 success-rate points on ScienceWorld. These gains are not uniform across ALFWorld subtasks: ECHO or RWML performs better on Cool and Pick2. COPE improves sample efficiency. Figure 1 compares COPE with GRPO on AppWorld, while Fig. 3 compares COPE with ECHO and GRPO on ScienceWorld. Overall, COPE is 1.6 and 2.0 more sample-efficient than GRPO on AppWorld and ScienceWorld, respectively. On ScienceWorld, ECHO requires 53 and 114 steps to reach equivalent performance milestones (making COPE 1.7 to 1.9 faster). This acceleration is even more pronounced at higher reward tiers: COPE achieves 0.6 reward by step 86, level neither baseline reaches within the first 150 steps. Thus, the multi-step action forecasting loss not only accelerates early-stage learning but also enables the policy to reach higher performance level under the same budget. COPE introduces little training overhead. Because COPE adds supervised pass over successful rollouts, its direct cost scales with the batch success rate. On ScienceWorld, this pass adds 11% time per training step on average, while shorter rollouts reduce the measured endto-end step time by 9% compared with GRPO  (Fig. 4)  .

Lazzati et al. (2026) traces the benefits of action chunking in robot imitation learning (Zhao et al., 2023) to delayed prediction: prediction of at has delay if made without the last observations. sections.title: 10 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced COPE, which trains language agent to forecast its own future actions alongside acting. Rather than fitting noisy observations, COPE trains on the success-filtered action chunk at:t+K, combining the current-action target with forecasts up to steps in the future. Across five benchmarks, COPE improves aggregate results over RL baselines. It also improves sample efficiency with little computational overhead. We hope this work motivates further methods for sample-efficient long-horizon agentic RL.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work introduces COPE, training algorithm for improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning for LLM-based agents; it is methodological contribution rather than deployed system, and its societal impact is largely mediated by how downstream practitioners apply it. All experiments are conducted on standard agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, τ 2-bench, and AppWorld) using open-weight or proprietary models strictly for research evaluation; the work does not involve human subjects, crowdsourcing, or the collection of new personal data. By coupling action forecasting and policy optimization within single backbone, COPE can reduce environmentinteraction costs without training or serving separate world model, lowering the barrier for resourceconstrained groups to study long-horizon LLM agents. We also note that, like other advances in sample-efficient agentic RL, more capable autonomous agents could in principle be misused for tasks such as automated misinformation or unauthorized web automation; practitioners building on COPE in higher-stakes domains should pair it with appropriate safety evaluation, deployment-time monitoring, and human oversight.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with method development and proof writing; to provide feedback on experimental design, including the separated-forecaster and implicit-ensembling analysis in Sec. 8; to help interpret experimental results; and to implement parts of the training and evaluation code. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets, clean or reformat datasets, perform translation, or conduct qualitative data analysis. We also used generative AI tools to draft and edit text for clarity, suggest section organization, search for and summarize related literature, and format references. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted derivations, code, reported results, and citations and take responsibility for the final content.

We train on 3,930 of them and test on 200. The two sets are disjoint and together cover 59.8% of the pool. Note that the commonly quoted WebShop figures 12,087 human-written instructions, 500-instruction test set, the full product catalogue describe different configuration and are not comparable to ours. SciWorld. SciWorld is our abbreviation for ScienceWorld. The environment defines 30 task types; the server excludes seven of them (task ids 5-1, 5-2, 9-1, 9-2, 9-3, 10-1, 10-2) and enumerates every variation of the remaining 23, giving pool of 4,639 (task type, variation) pairs indexed by single running id. We train on 2,120 of these and test on 200. The training ids cover 22 of the 23 task types and the test ids cover 12. τ 2-Bench. τ 2-Bench ships its own train/test partition per domain, and we use all three domains together: retail (74 train, 40 test), airline (30, 20) and telecom (74, 40), i.e. 178 training and 100 test tasks. We first compute the metric separately for each domain and report their unweighted arithmetic mean, so retail, airline, and telecom contribute equally despite their different test-set sizes. The environment server is launched with TAU2_DOMAIN=retail+airline+telecom and the split selected by TAU2_TASK_SPLIT; task ids are positional across the concatenated domains in that order, and the id files are generated from the same loaders the server uses (scripts/make_tau2_itemid.py), so row cannot name one task and train on another. Each task pairs customer goal with database state and set of state-based assertions, and every episode also runs simulated customer implemented with GPT-4o-mini at temperature 0.7. The resulting environment is stochastic, and τ 2 task is substantially more expensive than an ALFWorld or WebShop one which is why its pool is roughly one order of magnitude smaller. AppWorld. AppWorld ships four splits and we use its own partition unchanged, read with appworld.load_task_ids: train (90 tasks), dev (57), test_normal (168) and test_challenge (417), 732 in total. We train on train and evaluate on both test splits, which the evaluation harness runs as separate passes because the environment servers have to be restarted per split (APPWORLD_SPLIT selects the task list). test_challenge is not harder sample of the same distribution: it is built from scenarios held out entirely, so it measures transfer to unseen app combinations rather than to unseen instances of seen ones. An AppWorld task is Python REPL session against nine simulated apps and is scored by state-based unit tests, so success is all-or-nothing per task; with 90 training tasks it is by far the smallest training pool of the five environments.

sections.title: B EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 BASELINE METHODS We compare our method with prompting and training baselines spanning verbal self-reflection, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, online reinforcement learning, and observation-space predictive supervision. Reflexion. Reflexion is prompting baseline that asks the agent to verbally reflect on failed trial and uses the resulting reflection to guide subsequent attempt, without updating model parameters. We apply Reflexion to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld. RFT. Rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) samples trajectories, retains those that succeed, and fine-tunes the policy by maximum likelihood on their action tokens. Unlike GRPO, it treats the retained trajectories as supervised targets rather than optimizing group-relative policy-gradient objective. We evaluate RFT on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld. GRPO. GRPO is an online reinforcement learning baseline. For each training query, the actor samples group of trajectories from the current policy and optimizes the policy using group-relative advantages. Different from critic-based PPO, GRPO estimates advantages within each sampled group and therefore avoids training an additional value model. In our experiments, GRPO is applied to ALFWorld, WebShop, SciWorld, τ 2-Bench, and AppWorld.

The published AppWorld RL baseline numbers reported by G2PO use only difficulty-1/2 tasks: 72 training tasks and 105 tasks from test_normal, whereas we train on all 90 tasks and evaluate the complete test_normal (168) and test_challenge (417) splits. The reported setup also randomly samples its validation pool and differs from ours in prompt, history, and output formats, generation limits (512 versus 1,024 tokens per turn), and training length (50 versus 100 steps). These published numbers are therefore not controlled comparisons; nevertheless, both GRPO (ours) and COPE achieve higher normal-split success rates despite our broader evaluation set. RWML. RWML is two-stage world-model-based baseline. In the first stage, the backbone is trained on pre-collected (ht, at, ot+1) triplets to predict the next state, using rewards derived from matching the predicted and actual states. In the second stage, the resulting model is optimized with standard online GRPO on the task reward. Unlike ECHO and COPE, its world-model objective is applied only before policy optimization rather than alongside it. ECHO. ECHO is world-model-augmented reinforcement learning baseline that combines the GRPO loss on action tokens with an auxiliary cross-entropy loss on environment-observation tokens. It reuses the same rollouts, model backbone, and forward-pass logits as policy optimization, thereby providing dense predictive supervision without additional environment interactions or separately pretrained world model. Unlike RWML, which learns its world model from offline trajectory data before policy optimization, ECHO couples observation-space world modeling directly with online policy updates. We use the same GRPO hyperparameters for ECHO and set the environmentprediction coefficient to 0.01 on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld. EMPG. EMPG is an entropy-modulated policy gradient baseline that re-calibrates the learning signal based on step-wise predictive uncertainty. Unlike standard policy gradients, where update magnitude is implicitly coupled with action entropy, EMPG amplifies updates for confident correct actions, penalizes confident errors, and attenuates updates from uncertain steps. An additional futureclarity bonus encourages the agent toward lower-entropy next states. In our experiments, we apply EMPG on top of GRPO and evaluate it on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld.
